Question 1: Compare KNN and logistic regression

Use breast-cancer.csv, which contains 569 cases from the Wisconsin Diagnostic Breast Cancer dataset. Predict y (1 for malignant and 0 for benign) using mean_radius, mean_texture, and mean_smoothness.

Set a random seed and randomly split the observations into 70% training and 30% test data. Use the same split for every model. Standardize the predictors using the training means and standard deviations, and apply the same transformations to the test data.

Fit ordinary logistic regression with an intercept and no penalty, and KNN with Euclidean distance, equal neighbor weights, and

k∈{5,15,25,35,45}. k\in\{5,15,25,35,45\}.

Using the estimated probabilities for y = 1 on the test data, plot all six ROC curves in one figure and report their AUC values. Which of the six fitted models do you prefer? Give a brief justification based on your results.

Answer

I used seed 432506 and a stratified 70/30 random split, which gave 398 training observations and 171 test observations. I estimated the standardization parameters using only the training data.

logistic_model = LogisticRegression(C=np.inf, solver="lbfgs", max_iter=10000)
logistic_model.fit(X_train_std, y_train)

q1_probabilities = {
    "Logistic regression": logistic_model.predict_proba(X_test_std)[:, 1]
}

for k in [5, 15, 25, 35, 45]:
    model = KNeighborsClassifier(
        n_neighbors=k,
        metric="euclidean",
        weights="uniform",
    )
    model.fit(X_train_std, y_train)
    q1_probabilities[f"{k}-NN"] = model.predict_proba(X_test_std)[:, 1]

q1_auc = {
    model_name: roc_auc_score(y_test, probabilities)
    for model_name, probabilities in q1_probabilities.items()
}

q1_auc_table = pd.DataFrame(
    {"model": q1_auc.keys(), "test AUC": q1_auc.values()}
)
display(q1_auc_table.style.format({"test AUC": "{:.6f}"}).hide(axis="index"))
model test AUC
Logistic regression 0.974883
5-NN 0.937062
15-NN 0.972985
25-NN 0.973934
35-NN 0.977512
45-NN 0.978972 
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7.5, 5.5), constrained_layout=True)
colors = plt.cm.viridis(np.linspace(0.05, 0.95, len(q1_probabilities)))

for (model_name, probabilities), color in zip(q1_probabilities.items(), colors):
    false_positive_rate, true_positive_rate, _ = roc_curve(y_test, probabilities)
    ax.plot(
        false_positive_rate,
        true_positive_rate,
        linewidth=2,
        color=color,
        label=f"{model_name} (AUC = {q1_auc[model_name]:.4f})",
    )

ax.plot([0, 1], [0, 1], color="gray", linestyle="--", linewidth=1)
ax.set_title("Test ROC curves")
ax.set_xlabel("False positive rate")
ax.set_ylabel("True positive rate")
ax.set_xlim(0, 1)
ax.set_ylim(0, 1.01)
ax.grid(alpha=0.2)
ax.legend(frameon=False, loc="lower right")
plt.show()

I prefer 45-NN among these fitted models because it has the largest test AUC, 0.978972. Logistic regression is close, with an AUC of 0.974883, so the observed advantage of 45-NN is small and should not be treated as a general result beyond this split.

Question 2: Training and test ROC curves

Use the same data, training/test split, and standardization as in Question 1. Fit KNN with Euclidean distance, equal neighbor weights, and

k∈{1,3,5,10,20}. k\in\{1,3,5,10,20\}.

Use each fitted model to estimate probabilities for both the training and test observations. For training predictions, include each observation itself among its kk nearest neighbors.

For each kk, use a separate panel to show the training and test ROC curves together. Report both AUC values.

Explain the difference between training and test performance and how it changes with kk. In particular, explain what happens at k=1k=1 and why training performance may not reflect performance on new observations.

Answer

q2_k_values = [1, 3, 5, 10, 20]
q2_results = {}

for k in q2_k_values:
    model = KNeighborsClassifier(
        n_neighbors=k,
        metric="euclidean",
        weights="uniform",
    )
    model.fit(X_train_std, y_train)

    # Predicting on the training matrix includes each observation itself.
    train_probability = model.predict_proba(X_train_std)[:, 1]
    test_probability = model.predict_proba(X_test_std)[:, 1]
    q2_results[k] = {
        "train probability": train_probability,
        "test probability": test_probability,
        "train AUC": roc_auc_score(y_train, train_probability),
        "test AUC": roc_auc_score(y_test, test_probability),
    }

q2_auc_table = pd.DataFrame(
    [
        {
            "k": k,
            "training AUC": q2_results[k]["train AUC"],
            "test AUC": q2_results[k]["test AUC"],
        }
        for k in q2_k_values
    ]
)
display(
    q2_auc_table.style.format(
        {"training AUC": "{:.6f}", "test AUC": "{:.6f}"}
    ).hide(axis="index")
)
k training AUC test AUC
1 1.000000 0.861127
3 0.992649 0.926548
5 0.987622 0.937062
10 0.983041 0.959623
20 0.981068 0.974372 
fig, axes = plt.subplots(
    1, 5, figsize=(17, 3.5), sharex=True, sharey=True, constrained_layout=True
)

for ax, k in zip(axes, q2_k_values):
    train_fpr, train_tpr, _ = roc_curve(
        y_train, q2_results[k]["train probability"]
    )
    test_fpr, test_tpr, _ = roc_curve(
        y_test, q2_results[k]["test probability"]
    )
    ax.plot(
        train_fpr,
        train_tpr,
        linewidth=2,
        label=f"Train ({q2_results[k]['train AUC']:.3f})",
    )
    ax.plot(
        test_fpr,
        test_tpr,
        linewidth=2,
        linestyle="--",
        label=f"Test ({q2_results[k]['test AUC']:.3f})",
    )
    ax.plot([0, 1], [0, 1], color="gray", linestyle=":", linewidth=1)
    ax.set_title(f"k = {k}")
    ax.set_xlabel("False positive rate")
    ax.grid(alpha=0.2)
    ax.legend(frameon=False, fontsize=8, loc="lower right")

axes[0].set_ylabel("True positive rate")
plt.show()

Training AUC decreases from 1.000000 at k=1k=1 to 0.981068 at k=20k=20, while test AUC increases from 0.861127 to 0.974372 over the displayed values. The gap is especially large at k=1k=1. Because each training observation is included among its own neighbors, its nearest neighbor is itself, so 1-NN assigns every training observation its own class and obtains perfect training performance. A new observation cannot use itself as a neighbor, so this perfect fit does not carry over to the test data. Increasing kk averages over a larger neighborhood, which reduces the model’s sensitivity to individual training observations and improves test performance in this split.

1. Mistake selected

I reviewed sophiastierwalt’s Homework 05, Question 4(c). The selected item is the calculation used to support the statement that Euclidean and Manhattan 5NN misclassified 11 of the same images. The filter does not calculate the intersection of the two methods’ error sets.

2. Assessment

both = compare_manhattan_euc %>%
  filter(
    (pred_manhattan != pred_euclidean) &
    (pred_euclidean != y_test)
  )

“Together, they misidentified 11 of the same photos.”

The first condition, pred_manhattan != pred_euclidean, means the two distance metrics produced conflicting predictions (they disagree). The second condition, pred_euclidean != y_test, means Euclidean distance misclassified the image. However, the code does not directly check whether Manhattan distance also got the prediction wrong (pred_manhattan != y_test). For example, consider a test image with true label 1, Euclidean prediction 2, and Manhattan prediction 1. Under the original filtering condition, this observation would be selected because Euclidean distance failed (2≠12 \neq 1) and the two methods gave different results (1≠21 \neq 2), even though Manhattan distance actually classified it correctly. Therefore, the value 11 cannot be interpreted as the total number of photos misclassified by both methods. A more appropriate condition would need to check (pred_manhattan != y_test) & (pred_euclidean != y_test)

3. Correction and revision plan

The shared-error set should be calculated by requiring both predictions to differ from the true label:

both_misclassified = compare_manhattan_euc %>%
  filter(
    (pred_manhattan != y_test) &
    (pred_euclidean != y_test)
  )

dim(both_misclassified)
# [1] 58  3

The corrected interpretation is: Euclidean and Manhattan 5NN both misclassified 58 of the same test images. They do not necessarily assign the same incorrect label to every shared error. The report should replace the disagreement condition with the two error conditions, report 58 instead of 11, and revise the surrounding sentence accordingly.
